lead_verbatim: Five companies presented gene therapies, a transthyretin silencer and an oral myosin inhibitor for inherited and rare cardiomyopathies, and a patient treated with a gene therapy spoke by video link. The session's evidence was early: the largest gene therapy cohort was 12 patients, and the only phase 3 result presented, for the oral drug, rested on an exercise endpoint that many patients with advanced disease cannot perform.

presentations.paragraph_verbatim: Whitlock presented CAL-201, an intravenous gene therapy delivering MYBPC3 for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy caused by variants in that gene, which he said account for "about 40%" of genotyped disease. 1 In the phase 1/2 CALLISTO-HCM study 12 patients have been dosed in three cohorts, with 12 weeks of prophylactic immunosuppression. He reported a 44% reduction in NT-proBNP at six months in the second cohort and no dose-limiting toxicities; a 9 g/m2 reduction in left ventricular mass index appeared on the slide and was not spoken. 2 The slide listed an expedited designation in the US and priority status in the EU. The pivotal CALLISTO-2 study is planned for the second half of 2027 with a readout in 2029. He referred to "around 300 patients" in a natural history study, a figure given only in speech.

presentations.paragraph_verbatim: Petrov presented dromalsiran, a quarterly subcutaneous siRNA silencing transthyretin, for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. The phase 3 LODESTAR-2 study of 640 patients has a composite primary endpoint of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events at 30 months, and reported transthyretin knockdown of 91%. 5 The readout is expected "early next year"; the slide gives the first quarter of 2027. Petrov stated that health technology appraisal bodies do not accept biomarker knockdown as evidence of benefit, which is why the trial measures outcomes. He described a pipeline of "eight" programmes; the slide lists seven.

presentations.paragraph_verbatim: Nakamura presented tovacamten, a once-daily oral cardiac myosin inhibitor for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Kessler is a wholly owned subsidiary of Thornbury Pharma; the slide gives the completion of that transaction as 2 September 2026. In the phase 3 ORCHARD-HCM study of 212 patients, randomised 1:1 over 24 weeks, peak oxygen uptake improved by 1.9 mL/kg/min against placebo (p<0.001), with a 48 mmHg reduction in outflow tract gradient at the 14 mg dose. 6 A gain of 9.1 points on the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire appeared on the slide. In the phase 2 ORCHARD-1 study in non-obstructive disease she described "a signal"; the slide gives a gain of 0.8 mL/kg/min with p=0.238. A filing in the EU is planned for the second quarter of 2027, shown on the slide. She introduced herself as chief medical officer; her title slide reads senior vice president, clinical development.

presentations.paragraph_verbatim: Brandt presented ORL-7, a gene-agnostic intravenous gene therapy expressing a protective modifier for genetic dilated cardiomyopathy. In the phase 1/2 LANTERNWAY study of 9 patients, ejection fraction improved by at least 6 points in 5 of 9 at six months, which he described as "most patients", with no safety events "of note". 7 Two further programmes, BEACONFIELD and WAYFARER, appeared on the slide without their indications. He stated that the company has raised "about $180 million" and operates its own central testing laboratory.

paragraphs.verbatim: The panel, chaired by Professor Mette Kristiansen and Professor Alessandro Conti, added Yusuf Demir of Castlebay Therapeutics and Professor Robert Ashcroft. Demir stated that in Castlebay's phase 1/2 study of CBY-01 for PRKAG2 syndrome "about two-thirds" of patients showed what he termed approvable levels of improvement in exercise capacity against almost none in the control group, without figures, and that a phase 3 study would start early next year. 8 Ashcroft stated that Harrowgate Therapeutics, which was not presenting, had announced two weeks earlier that its gene therapy for Fabry cardiomyopathy met its primary endpoint, and that he very much hopes for formal approval early next year, first in the US and then in Europe. Nothing is approved. He added that the first patient in that programme was treated in 2017 and that over 200 patients are in a natural history study, both spoken only.
Whitlock offered an anecdote in support of the safety of reducing the target protein: two siblings with no functional protein at all, which in his view makes an 80% reduction safe.

Nakamura said that "about 10" interventional trials are running in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; whether ORCHARD-HCM itself is complete or ongoing was left unclear, the slide saying "ongoing". The panel agreed that peak oxygen uptake is becoming the pivotal endpoint across the field, and that many patients with advanced disease cannot perform the test: only 2 of the 9 patients in LANTERNWAY completed it.

guest_speaker.name: Mateus Oliveira
guest_speaker.paragraph_verbatim: Mateus Oliveira, 27, from Portugal, who has Danon disease, joined by video link, introduced by Dr Henrik Solberg. He said that at 19 he was told he would need a transplant, and that about three years ago he received a gene therapy; he did not name the product or the company, and the report does not. He described the change in his own terms: he can climb the stairs at university "without stopping on the landing", and "it's the small things". He said he hopes the treatment "has bought me 10 to 15 years" and that he does not know "if it's forever". 9 He gave no clinical measurements, and none are added here.
